title: Who ran it, and who ended it
lede: Roles and dates come from the filings and reports cited in each entry. We name only people whose part we could source; the executives who built Redbox inside McDonald’s are not named in the documents we read.

people.name: Greg Waring
people.text: Spoke for Redbox when it was still a McDonald’s subsidiary with 750 machines, and predicted a day when it would be in “the vast majority” of the chain’s more than 13,000 U.S. restaurants.[^3]

people.name: Paul Davis
people.text: Named in the published description of a 2011 CNN interview titled “Redbox: DVDs are not dead.” A 2010 interview on the same channel, credited to “the CEO of Coinstar”, is titled “Redbox: We will stream movies.”[^37]

people.name: Erik E. Prusch
people.text: Signed the sale to Apollo’s funds and called Apollo “an ideal partner.”[^14]

people.name: David Sambur
people.text: Spoke for the buyer in 2016: “We are extremely excited for our funds to acquire Outerwall.”[^14]

people.name: Galen C. Smith
people.text: Outerwall’s chief financial officer from 2013 to 2016, having joined in 2009. He led Redbox through the Apollo years and the 2021 listing.[^17]

people.name: William J. Rouhana Jr.
people.role: Chairman and chief executive, Chicken Soup for the Soul Entertainment
people.text: Bought Redbox in 2022. The only director left after the controlling shareholder removed the board on June 11, 2024; Variety reported that he stepped down as chief executive on June 24. In his declaration to the court he blamed the lenders’ “refusals” to meet their obligations.[^24][^26]

people.name: Thomas M. Horan
people.role: Judge, U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware
people.text: Converted the case to Chapter 7 on July 10, 2024.[^26]

people.name: George L. Miller
people.text: Responsible for liquidating the estate, including the proposed sale of its copyright litigation rights.[^34]
